articles.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
articles.summary: If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.
articles.body:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.

This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.

Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.

The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea

Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.

In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.

The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".

The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.

Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.

Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.

North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.

In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.

TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.

Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.

The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.

"Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.

Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.

If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.

Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.

In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.

As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

articles.title: Trump's tariffs could shut this Canadian town. Its residents are fighting to save it
articles.summary: A century-old paper mill in Témiscaming, Quebec is indefinitely closed after the US imposed 50% tariffs on its products, putting hundreds out of work.
articles.body:
As you cross the Ottawa river into Témiscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon.

The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country.

Most of the mill‘s 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief.

For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life.

She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year.

"It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack".

In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period".

Property values in Témiscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town.

There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out.

"If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers.

"There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary."

At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth.

But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of Témiscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive.

"If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,” says Stéphane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill.

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?

White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom

That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people.

The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it.

They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France.

The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017.

"We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall.

But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support.

Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge.

In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers.

Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada".

He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free.

And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken".

"We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back."

Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos.

This month, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure.

Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024.

Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; £4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said.

Sébastien Lemire, the elected MP for Témiscaming from the Bloc Québécois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly.

A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas.

It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets.

On the Témiscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars."

In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes.

Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs.

The Témiscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US.

Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in Témiscaming.

Frank Dottori has been through all of this before.

Now in his 80s and retired in Témiscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO.

Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support.

But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma.

Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold.

"Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they if they organise themselves," he said.

It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term.

Many workers in Témiscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump — whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls — to ease some of his tariffs on Canada.

"We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too."

There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at Témiscaming's mill, however.

Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult.

In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens.

"We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."

articles.title: Ebola death toll in DR Congo passes 5,000
articles.summary: Authorities are struggling to find a way to control the ⁠outbreak, with no approved treatments or vaccines.
articles.body:
The death ⁠toll ⁠from Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 5,000, government data ⁠show, with authorities yet to find a way to control the ⁠country’s deadliest outbreak of the virus on record.

The latest death toll was announced on Friday.

Ebola has infected more than 10,000 people in the DRC since the outbreak was declared in May.

There are no approved treatments or vaccines to combat the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus, responsible for the ongoing outbreak.

Delayed detection, conflict and strained health services have helped the virus spread more rapidly than in past outbreaks, reaching eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces to date.

The virus has spread to neighbouring countries as well.

Last week, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case , extending the outbreak’s geographic ‌spread to West Africa. East African countries Kenya and Uganda have also reported cases.

This year’s Ebola outbreak is the second-largest ever, behind only the 2014-2016 epidemic that infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than ⁠11,000 people across Guinea, Liberia ⁠and Sierra Leone.

Some governments have been restricting travel to affected countries or quarantining travellers who have recently visited or transited through them.

On Friday, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from Kenya, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

The measures include suspending travel by Saudi citizens to Kenya and a pause on issuing all types of visas to travellers from the country.

The kingdom is also prohibiting entry to travellers arriving from Kenya, including those transiting through third countries who have stayed in Kenya or other Ebola-affected countries within the previous 21 days.

In June, Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and entry from the DRC, Uganda, and South Sudan.

articles.title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations
articles.summary: The prime minister says Britain must "face up to the past" for its role in the transatlantic slave trade but reparations are "not the right answer".
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "open" to the possibility of the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out considering financial reparations.

Burham said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected by the slave trade" and was open to "calls for an apology".

He dismissed the idea of paying financial reparations, saying they were "not the right answer".

The comments come ahead of a Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean next week, which Burnham will attend. Caribbean nations have renewed calls for the UK to apologise for its role in the slave trade, and for reparations, as King Charles III tours the region .

Burham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

"I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in his piece for the Guardian .

He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". Burnham said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue" adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."

A government source told the BBC this was "morally the right thing to do".

Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.

Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow.

Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.

Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough.

"The British Government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now. This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice," he said.

From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.

Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.

As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of their slaves.

The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

articles.title: Big Bang Theory creator Chuck Lorre’s Los Angeles charity campus broke ground on its final building on October 29, after opening a new kitchen in February, as its nonprofit delivers 1.5 million meals a year
articles.summary: A major expansion of a Los Angeles charity backed by The Big Bang Theory creator Chuck Lorre reached another milestone on October 29, 2026, when Project
articles.body: A major expansion of a Los Angeles charity backed by The Big Bang Theory creator Chuck Lorre reached another milestone on October 29, 2026, when Project Angel Food broke ground on the final building of its new campus. The organisation, which prepares and delivers medically tailored meals to people living with serious illnesses, is developing the two-building facility with support from The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation. According to Project Angel Food’s official announcement, the new Community Outreach Center will bring client services, nutrition education, volunteer facilities and research programmes together at its Hollywood site. The development follows the opening of the campus kitchen in February.Final building begins construction at Hollywood campusThe groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of the second and final phase of The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation Kitchen and Campus, located across 922 and 960 Vine Street in Hollywood. Chuck Lorre joined Project Angel Food CEO Richard Ayoub, Trisha Cardoso, president and chief giving officer of The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation, California State Senator Ben Allen, board member Mary Fisher, donors and volunteers for the event.The new building, known as the Community Outreach Center, is intended to complement the expanded kitchen and operations facility that opened on February 5, 2026. While the first building focuses on preparing, storing and distributing meals, the second will provide space for the services and programmes that support clients beyond food delivery. Project Angel Food said the centre will include expanded client and nutrition services, a demonstration kitchen, volunteer facilities, a rooftop herb garden and a Research and Policy Institute. The campus is designed to bring meal production, education, research and direct support together in one location.New kitchen increases meal production capacityThe first building's opening in February marked a significant expansion of Project Angel Food's operations. The new Kitchen and Operations Center more than doubled the organisation's culinary space, increasing it from approximately 7,700 square feet to 16,000 square feet. The upgraded facility also expanded its cooking infrastructure. The kitchen now has three hot cook lines, compared with one previously, along with 90 burners and 21 ovens. These changes are expected to increase annual production capacity from around 1.5 million meals to more than 4.5 million medically tailored meals.The expansion also strengthens storage and distribution. The organisation increased its freezer space and dry storage, while enlarging its packing and distribution areas. This allows it to maintain a frozen meal reserve of up to three weeks, compared with approximately two days previously, helping protect deliveries during emergencies and disruptions. Project Angel Food prepares and delivers approximately 1.5 million medically tailored meals annually to clients across Los Angeles County. Its meals are designed to address the nutritional needs of people dealing with critical and life-threatening illnesses.Outreach centre to focus on nutrition and researchThe Community Outreach Center will extend the organisation's work beyond meal preparation. Expanded client and nutrition services areas will allow staff to assess people's dietary needs, connect them with suitable meals and provide additional support. A demonstration kitchen, called Founders Hall, will offer practical cooking and nutrition education to clients, caregivers, physicians and other organisations working to address food insecurity. The programmes are intended to help people understand how to prepare nutritious meals and, where their health improves, support their transition from receiving fully prepared meals to cooking independently.The building will also include a rooftop herb garden, providing space for community activities and growing fresh ingredients. Its Research and Policy Institute will focus on studying the outcomes of medically tailored meals, sharing findings and building support for wider coverage of such services through programmes including Medi-Cal and Medicare. The organisation's broader aim is to strengthen the role of nutrition in healthcare, particularly for people whose illnesses make access to appropriate food an important part of their treatment and recovery.Chuck Lorre's support helps drive the expansionThe campus is part of Project Angel Food's Rise to the Challenge campaign, a multi-year fundraising effort aimed at increasing the organisation's ability to serve people across Los Angeles County. The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation has been a major supporter of the project, helping make the expansion possible. At the groundbreaking, Lorre spoke about his personal connection to the importance of proper nutrition, saying he had experienced periods without food or healthy food himself. He described being part of an organisation working to address food insecurity as humbling.Project Angel Food CEO Richard Ayoub said the new centre would help the organisation become a national leader in the Food Is Medicine movement. He also announced that approximately $3 million remained to be raised through the campaign to complete the project. The organisation was founded in 1989 during the AIDS crisis and has since delivered more than 20 million meals. With the kitchen already operating and construction now beginning on the Community Outreach Center, the two-building campus is expected to be completed in 2028. Together, the facilities are intended to expand not only the number of meals Project Angel Food can prepare, but also the nutrition services, education, volunteer support and research available to the people it serves.You use AI every day. articles.title: US execution survivor Christa Pike says she is now in ‘constant pain’
articles.summary: Pike, 50, is being held in solitary confinement and faces an uncertain future after surviving a failed lethal injection.
articles.body:
An American woman who survived an execution in a Tennessee prison has spoken out for the first time.

In a statement released via her legal team on Friday, Christa Pike, 50, said she is now in constant pain and struggling to speak.

“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike said, adding that the pain is both “physical and emotional”.

“I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” Pike said.

Pike and her boyfriend tortured, stabbed and beat a 19-year-old classmate to death in 1995. As Pike was 18 at the time, she was handed the death sentence.

The victim’s mother travelled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution.

Pike said she “continues to think” about the victim’s family and the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.

Pike’s lawyers say the two separate doses of the lethal drug phenobarbital administered to her on September 30 may have failed to kill her because the drug did not enter her bloodstream. Instead, it pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.

Pike was hospitalised and unconscious for days following the botched execution.

Despite her ordeal, Pike remains scheduled to die, and is being held in solitary confinement in the interim.

Her legal team has asked a federal judge to allow her to interact with other prisoners, saying her isolation in the wake of the failed execution has caused “significant psychological harm and trauma”.

Her legal team has also asked Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to change her sentence to life in prison.

Last week, however, Lee told reporters that he “suspects” her sentence will be the same as before, “unless otherwise determined by the courts”.

The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences.

The Tennessee governor has organised an independent review of the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year.

Frank Strada, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution.

articles.title: Putin wants Africa on his side. African leaders are playing their own game
articles.summary: Russia is seeking allies and expanding its influence abroad as its war in Ukraine drags on. African governments, meanwhile, are cozying up to the Kremlin for reasons of their own.
articles.body: Russia is seeking allies and expanding its influence abroad as its war in Ukraine drags on. African governments, meanwhile, are cozying up to the Kremlin for reasons of their own. As he hosted the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow this week, President Vladimir Putin portrayed Russia as a better partner for Africa than the West, which he accused of exploiting the continent’s resources, maintaining a colonial approach and using debt to hold back development. Russia, he argued, offered a different model of cooperation, one which allowed both parties to prosper through closer ties in trade and technology. “Our business does not engage in the predatory, neo-colonial exploitation of natural and human resources,” Putin said, adding that Russian companies supported local job creation and tax revenues. Delegations from 48 of Africa’s 54 countries attended the two-day gathering. Twenty-two were represented by heads of state, according to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, compared with 17 at the 2023 summit and 43 at the first meeting in 2019. Such visibility helps Moscow counter its growing international isolation as it grapples with punitive Western sanctions. Will Brown, an Africa policy specialist at the European Council on Foreign Relations, says images of Putin alongside African leaders may matter more than what was agreed at the summit, since they can be reused by Russian influence networks to shape perceptions across Africa and the wider Global South. “The ‘story’ of the summit is the most important thing,” Brown told CNN. African governments, however, are not simply choosing between Moscow and the West. Tighisti Amare, director of the Africa Program at Chatham House, calls their approach “diversified non-alignment”: keeping ties with several partners rather than committing to one camp. Their reasons differ, she said. Some seek security support, others want agricultural supplies, energy investment, or diplomatic backing. Brown says many governments also use international competition to hedge their bets and secure better offers from Western partners. Security ties, different outcomes Russia has gained ground in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, where military-led governments turned to Moscow for military support after breaking with Western partners. Russia’s military role has grown through the Africa Corps, a paramilitary organization that assumed much of Wagner’s work after the mercenary group’s 2023 mutiny against the Kremlin. Russia has gained ground in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, where military-led governments turned to Moscow for military support after breaking with Western partners. Russia’s military role has grown through the Africa Corps, a paramilitary organization that assumed much of Wagner’s work after the mercenary group’s 2023 mutiny against the Kremlin. The Sahel, the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, is a key focus. Anna Ida Rock, a researcher at the Swedish Defense Research Agency, says Africa Corps has a reported presence in Burkina Faso, the Central African Republic (CAR), Equatorial Guinea, Libya, Mali and Niger. Russian military instructors have also been reported in the Republic of Congo, Madagascar and Togo, though claims about Togo are disputed. Moscow is also seeking a naval foothold on the Red Sea through a proposed naval facility in Sudan. The shift from Wagner to Africa Corps was more than a name change. The new force operates openly under Russia’s Defense Ministry and military intelligence. Many personnel are former Wagner fighters, but Africa Corps focuses more on training, advising and protecting strategic sites. Wagner remains active in CAR, whose government has resisted the transition. Results vary. In Mali, Russian forces helped the government retake the north-eastern city of Kidal, but insecurity has worsened and the Africa Corps has suffered significant losses. In Burkina Faso, Russian personnel have focused on protecting the government during political instability. Their role in Niger has been more limited. In CAR, Russian forces helped keep the government in power, but insecurity persists. The arrangement has helped the government secure its position, but many civilians do not feel safer. A smaller economic footprint Russia’s political and security presence in Africa is not matched by its trade with the continent. Trade was estimated at $27 billion in 2025, below the $40 billion target Moscow set in 2019. Putin has now set a new goal of more than $50 billion. China and the European Union are far larger trading partners for Africa. China-Africa trade reached about $348 billion in 2025, while trade between the EU and Africa stood at about $395 billion. Agriculture is one area where Russia has established stronger commercial ties. Putin said Russia exported 13 million metric tons of agricultural products to Africa in the first nine months of 2026 and highlighted fertilizer supplies. Energy is another area of cooperation, though projects remain at different stages. Russia’s state nuclear company, Rosatom, is building Egypt’s El Dabaa nuclear power plant, while talks about floating nuclear plants elsewhere have not reached construction. At the summit, Putin also promoted digital cooperation and local production of medicines and vaccines. But Amare says turning these proposals into tangible results will require investment, production facilities and skills. Arms and recruitment Ethiopia illustrates what Russia can still offer militarily. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said at the summit that his country had received Russian Su-35 fighter jets and would acquire four S-400 long-range air-defense systems. The deal comes as tensions and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raise concerns about a possible return to wider conflict. The agreement covers 12 aircraft. Russia’s state arms exporter told Reuters that it had delivered two. The deal’s value and the delivery schedule for the S-400s have not been disclosed. The deal shows that Moscow can supply advanced weapons despite Western sanctions, Rock told CNN, but noted it could concern Egypt, given tensions between Cairo and Addis Ababa over the Nile. Russia’s arms exports overall continue to decline. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute reports that Russian exports dropped 64% between 2016–2020 and 2021–2025, while the United States and China remained among the world’s largest suppliers. Closer military ties also carry risks. Amnesty International documented cases of Africans allegedly recruited into Russia’s military through deception, coercion and economic hardship. Amnesty said the circumstances in many cases amounted to trafficking. CNN interviewed African men who said they were misled or forced into Russian military service and sent to fight in Ukraine. Russia has denied involvement in the unlawful recruitment of Africans. In February, its embassy in Kenya said Russian authorities had never engaged in the illegal recruitment of Kenyan citizens while maintaining that foreign nationals could voluntarily enlist in its armed forces. Moscow’s promises and Africa’s calculations The summit produced a joint declaration, an agreement on civilian artificial intelligence and a 2027–2029 Russia-Africa action plan. The African Union Commission and Russia also signed a cooperation plan covering security, trade, energy, agriculture, health, education and technology. The Commission says it is a framework, not a legally binding agreement. Amare says progress will depend on whether the commitments receive funding, clear institutional responsibility and deadlines. Brown says African governments are navigating a harsher international environment but are finding ways to use it to their advantage, widening their options and pressing established partners to improve their offers. “They also see the increasingly nasty world we live in and the cards they have to play,” he says. Putin may be courting Africa, but Brown says many governments are “playing their hand very skillfully.”

articles.title: Woman who secretly returned from London without informing family found dead in Pune flat
articles.summary: PUNE: A 34-year-old woman whose family believed she was studying in London was found dead in a rented apartment in Pune, days after food delivery
articles.body: PUNE: A 34-year-old woman whose family believed she was studying in London was found dead in a rented apartment in Pune, days after food delivery transactions alerted her parents to the possibility that she had returned to India.Mugdha Deshmukh, a native of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, was found dead inside her apartment at the Lodha Belmondo residential complex in Gahunje, Pimpri Chinchwad, on Thursday. Police said there were no visible injury marks on her body.Mugdha had left for the UK in July 2025 to pursue an MBA. However, without informing her family, she returned to India in August and began living in the rented apartment, police said.According to investigators, Mugdha lived alone in London and had taken up part-time jobs. Her family remained in touch with her through phone calls and messages and believed she was still in the UK.Food delivery transactions raise suspicionThe family became concerned on October 24 when they were unable to contact Mugdha. Her mobile phone was subsequently switched off, her father Avinash Deshmukh stated in a complaint lodged with the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar police earlier this week.Her family then contacted a friend in London, who said the last communication with Mugdha had been through messages on October 22.The friend approached London police to report her missing but was informed that she had left the UK around the end of August, an official said.Concerned about her whereabouts, the family approached Indian authorities and the Indian High Commission for assistance.Mugdha's father also examined her bank statements and noticed several transactions between October 8 and 25 on food delivery and online service platforms.One of the transactions was suspected to have originated from the Osmanpura area of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, leading the family to suspect that she could be in India.The family subsequently approached the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar crime branch, fearing for her safety.Police trace apartment in PuneThe Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar police traced Mugdha's location to the Lodha Belmondo complex in Gahunje and alerted their counterparts in Pimpri Chinchwad."We reached the flat she was residing in, gained entry with the help of a keymaker, and found her dead inside," said senior inspector Devendra Chavan of Shirgaon Police in Pimpri Chinchwad.He added that there were no visible injury marks on the body, and her viscera was preserved to ascertain the exact cause of death.During the investigation, police found that Mugdha had rented the apartment in April but began living there only after returning from the UK in August.Police have launched a probe to establish the circumstances surrounding her death.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: Polish president turns plane around to return home as court chief’s suspension sparks protest
articles.summary: Police secured Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal on Friday as dozens of protesters gathered to demonstrate against what they perceive as the wrongful suspension of the top court’s president by the current pro-European government.
articles.body: Police secured Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal on Friday as dozens of protesters gathered to demonstrate against what they perceive as the wrongful suspension of the top court’s president by the current pro-European government. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers. Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was flying to Senegal, said he turned his flight back because of the situation. “At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I ⁠am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning,” he wrote on X. Poland’s top judicial bodies, including the Constitutional Tribunal, have been a major bone of contention between the current pro-European government and the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS). Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions, including the Constitutional Tribunal. The PiS reforms led the EU to impose fines on Poland. The pro-European government of Donald Tusk came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, the government’s efforts have been blocked by veto by two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki. The information about the suspension of the president of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Święczkowski, was published on the website of the court around 6 p.m. local time. The website of the Tribunal went down soon after so The Associated Press could not independently verify the official reasons given for his suspension. Święczkowski became head of the Constitutional Tribunal under the PiS government, and Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal. “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Prime Minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Speaking about the future of the Constitutional Tribunal at Campus Polska in August, Tusk said his government had a plan to ensure the tribunal would be again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging his methods may not be to everyone’s liking. Politicians from PiS, currently the largest opposition force, have criticized Święczkowski’s suspension. “This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X Friday evening. “That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless.”

articles.title: Joseph Kabila: Former president becomes DR Congo's latest rebel leader
articles.summary: What does Joseph Kabila launching a new rebel movement mean for DR Congo?
articles.body:
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.

In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.

His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.

When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.

Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.

For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.

For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.

But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.

Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.

"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.

Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.

"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.

Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.

The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.

Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.

And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.

While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.

His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.

There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.

"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a research group which campaigns against disinformation in that part of Africa.

Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.

He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.

Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.

But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".

Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.

"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.

In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.

And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.

Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.

Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.

"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."

Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

What's the fighting in DR Congo all about?

How Trump wants the US to cash in on mineral-rich DR Congo's peace deal

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.

The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.

From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.

He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.

At the time, he rejected the accusations.

Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.

In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.

The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.

From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.

However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.

Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.

"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.

Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.

"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.

Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.

Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.

Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.

Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.

"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.

International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.

"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.

articles.title: US greenlights $2.1bn Patriot missile sale to Ukraine
articles.summary: Deal would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since Trump took office in 2025.
articles.body:
The United States says it has approved the possible sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine ⁠for an estimated $2.1bn.

The package of missiles, parts and support, announced on Friday by the US State Department, would be one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to Kyiv since the start of the second administration of President Donald Trump in January 2025.

The Patriot system is the most effective weapon to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles.

Delayed missile deliveries, however, have stoked US-Ukraine tensions after Trump announced a diesel deal ⁠with Russia and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for his unwillingness to stop attacks on Russian refineries.

Ukraine has long said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to knock down the growing waves of missiles Russia’s military fires at the country.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for Washington to sign off on critical missile supplies, as Russia stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian energy and civilian infrastructure.

A Russian drone strike on Thursday killed at least 14 people on a crowded rail platform in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro.

Five people were killed in daytime strikes on two other cities, and a late-evening missile strike killed one person in the capital, Kyiv, officials said.

Despite Ukraine’s need for quick deliveries of the missiles, Kyiv is unlikely to receive the Patriot interceptors soon. Weapons sales typically take years to fulfil.

Two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles, which have yet to be made, are not expected to be delivered until a couple of years into the 2030s.

Ukraine will pay for the missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway through a programme called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union’s Ukraine Support Loan, the State Department said in its statement.

US weapons manufacturer Lockheed Martin is the principal contractor for the sale ⁠of the Patriot interceptors.

The US Army awarded Lockheed a contract worth up to $58.6bn to produce Patriot interceptor missiles in July.

Lockheed has said the deal ‌would allow it to follow through on a promise to triple PAC-3 production capacity by the end of 2030. It has previously announced that Patriot PAC-3 missile interceptor production would reach ‌2,000 units ‌annually.

Pentagon negotiators are pressing weapons contractors to speed up production.

The US military’s supply of large quantities of weapons to allies and its own heavy munitions use for its operations in Iran have raised concerns about its inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.

articles.title: Halloween and Pitru Paksha: How East and West Honour the Departed Differently
articles.summary: Three weeks ago, many Indian families sat on the floor with sesame seeds, kusha grass, and a brass vessel of water, offering tarpan to parents and
articles.body: Three weeks ago, many Indian families sat on the floor with sesame seeds, kusha grass, and a brass vessel of water, offering tarpan to parents and grandparents no longer here. This Saturday, families in America and Europe will hang paper skeletons on their doors and send children out in costumes to collect sweets. Both customs are, at their heart, about the dead. Yet one is quiet and solemn, and the other is noisy and playful. Side by side, they show how differently two cultures make peace with the people they’ve lost.Two Calendars, One SeasonPitru Paksha follows the lunar calendar. It’s the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada or Ashwin, depending on the regional calendar. In 2026, it ran from late September and ended on October 10 with Mahalaya Amavasya, the new moon.Halloween falls on October 31 on the solar calendar, followed by All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day on November 1 and 2.Even so, both fall in early autumn in the northern hemisphere. The harvest is done. Days are shortening. Across many cultures, this time of year has been linked with the dead returning, perhaps because nature itself seems to be dying back.Pitru Paksha: Feeding and ThankingThe core belief behind Pitru Paksha is that ancestors live in Pitru Loka, the realm of the forefathers, and depend on their descendants for nourishment and peace. During this fortnight, they’re believed to come close to the earth.Families perform shraddh on the tithi of a particular ancestor's passing. Tarpan involves offering water mixed with black sesame, often while standing in a river or facing south. Pinda, rice balls mixed with sesame and ghee, are offered as food for the departed.Crows are fed, since they’re seen as messengers of the ancestors. Brahmins, cows and the poor are also given food. The mood is serious and grateful. Many families avoid buying new things, starting ventures or holding celebrations during the fortnight, since it’s a time devoted to the past rather than to new beginnings.A sense of debt drives this. Hindu thought speaks of pitru rin, the debt owed to ancestors for life itself. Shraddh is one way to repay it.Halloween: Remembering and Playing With FearHalloween comes from a different view. Its oldest roots lie in beliefs that the dead and other spirits wandered freely at this time of year, and that not all of them were friendly. Disguises, lanterns and offerings were partly protective.Christian observances layered remembrance on top. All Souls’ Day, on November 2, remains a day for prayers and candles on graves in many Catholic countries.But modern Halloween, especially in North America, has turned fear into fun. Children dress as ghosts and witches. Haunted houses sell tickets. The dead become characters in a playful show, rather than relatives to be fed.That doesn’t mean the Western approach is shallow. Laughing at death can be a way of facing it. And many families still visit cemeteries or light candles for loved ones around this time.Where the Two Traditions MeetDespite the differences, the overlap is striking. Both believe the dead come close at this time of year. Both involve offering food, whether pinda and kheer or, in older European custom, soul cakes and plates left out overnight.Both use light. In India, Diwali lamps, which follow Pitru Paksha within a few weeks, are traditionally said to light the way for ancestors returning to their realm. Some families hang an akash deep, a high lantern, through the month of Kartik for this purpose. In the West, candles in windows and on graves serve a similar role.And both, in the end, are about not forgetting. Whether through a solemn tarpan at a riverbank or a child in a sheet asking for sweets, the dead are kept in the conversation.This year, Halloween falls during Scorpio season, with the Sun and a retrograde Mercury both in that sign. Astrologically, Scorpio rules endings, inheritance and the bonds that survive death, a fitting backdrop for any tradition that honours the departed.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. articles.title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
articles.summary: The home secretary has faced opposition from within the government over plans to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.
articles.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.

She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care.

The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.

Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.

Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.

In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.

But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.

But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.

The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.

The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.

In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

articles.title: 'Real danger, real need': Why Zelenskyy wants Patriot missiles before winter
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ukraine is racing to secure hundreds of Patriot air defence interceptors before winter, as Russia intensifies attacks on critical
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ukraine is racing to secure hundreds of Patriot air defence interceptors before winter, as Russia intensifies attacks on critical infrastructure and Kyiv faces growing uncertainty over the availability of missiles from the United States and its European allies.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the announcement of a proposed $2.1 billion arrangement involving 500 Patriot interceptors but expressed concern that deliveries could take years. Kyiv wants its partners to release missiles from their existing stockpiles immediately, arguing that the coming winter could leave millions of people vulnerable to Russian strikes on electricity, heating, water supply and transport networks.The urgency stems from Ukraine's limited ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. While the country has other air defence systems to counter drones and cruise missiles, Patriot systems remain among its few effective defences against fast-moving ballistic weapons.Damage to power stations and heating infrastructure becomes particularly dangerous when temperatures fall below freezing. Disruptions to electricity, water and heating can affect not only military operations but also civilian life, making energy infrastructure a key vulnerability as winter approaches.The first two weeks of October reportedly saw more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of Ukraine's power grid.Zelenskyy has said Ukraine needs to be in a stronger position during negotiations and prevent Russia from breaking life in Ukrainian cities and communities. He has argued that this would only be possible if Kyiv had enough resources to defend itself.“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy said in an X post.“We are asking for decisions that can guarantee the protection of lives not the day after tomorrow or sometime later, but at the very moment the threat is there,” he added.Kyiv has asked its American partners for a winter support package involving 100 Patriot interceptors a month.“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” Zelenskyy said.He has proposed that the US and its partners supply Ukraine with interceptors from their existing stocks during the winter and replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and its partners.“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” he said, adding that supplying them immediately and replenishing the stocks later would be “entirely feasible”.Europe's stockpile dilemmaUkraine's demand for Patriot missiles is putting pressure on European countries, which have already supplied Kyiv with military equipment and financial assistance. Several of its leading European backers, however, are now facing a difficult choice between meeting Ukraine's urgent requirements and retaining enough interceptors to protect their own territory.Germany, one of Kyiv's biggest military aid donors, has transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. Berlin has supplied three systems from its military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the US would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands has also assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles.But European governments are increasingly concerned about the availability of interceptors. Germany must balance Ukraine's needs against the minimum stockpiles required to protect its own territory and meet its Nato commitments.“We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defence ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin after the NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.”Norwegian defence minister Tore O. Sandvik has also cautioned against placing the long-term burden of military assistance on Europe.“I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” he told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.”The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors, which Ukraine relies on to counter Russian ballistic missiles. Kyiv is developing its own Freyja interceptor, but the system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can take on that role.Until then, Ukraine needs an immediate supply of Patriot missiles.“One of the priority directions is Patriot — PAC-3 or PAC-2,” Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told POLITICO. “The first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.”The shortage is also linked to competing demands on US supplies. Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in the US, making Washington central to decisions on their sale, supply and future production.US President Donald Trump had raised hopes at the Ankara summit by indicating that Ukraine could be allowed to produce US-designed Patriot interceptors under licence. Such an arrangement could eventually reduce Kyiv's dependence on American deliveries, but it would not address the immediate shortage.US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said a long-term production agreement would not be concluded before winter, while manufacturing the first missiles would take longer.Trump subsequently appeared to step back from the proposal, saying last week: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."The war involving Iran has added pressure on US missile supplies, with Washington also seeking to replenish its own stocks. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy's calls for more Patriot missiles, Trump said: “We want missiles too.”Ukraine has also signed an agreement to receive PAC-2 interceptors being manufactured in Germany, although deliveries are unlikely before next year.Pressure on Europe's arsenalsThe shortage has pushed Kyiv and its partners to look for interceptors across European military stockpiles. Countries such as Poland, Spain and Greece are among those facing pressure to contribute, but their willingness to release missiles varies according to their own defence requirements.Poland confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors following requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior US commanders. Polish media outlet Defence24 reported that only five missiles were transferred.The decision triggered a political backlash, with opposition lawmakers accusing the government of weakening Poland's defences at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly crossed or strayed into its territory.Countries closer to Russia are also reluctant to reduce their existing stocks, with their armed forces already considering their air defences insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat cited by POLITICO.This has shifted attention towards Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine's military effort than Germany and several Northern European donors.Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or quantity. Greece has not announced any Patriot transfers. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested up to 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens.Kyiv has continued to negotiate with its partners to secure whatever missiles they can spare. During an earlier effort, Ukrainian officials and Rutte approached European governments with requests for interceptors from their existing stocks.“Dear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?” former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov recalled asking.Berlin also offered to contribute additional missiles if other countries released some from their stockpiles.“If you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,” Fedorov quoted German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. “That’s the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.”Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said Kyiv is struggling to buy, exchange or secure available interceptors amid rising demand in the Middle East and the need for the US and European countries to replenish their own supplies.“We are literally fighting for every missile,” Sybiha said.Ukraine war adds to Europe's economic strainThe pressure to sustain military assistance to Ukraine comes as European governments face economic challenges, including high energy costs and inflation. The disruption of Russian gas supplies following the invasion of Ukraine has forced several countries, particularly Germany, to rethink their energy arrangements and seek alternative sources.The additional pressure on energy markets following the Iran war has added to concerns over fuel costs and household expenses.Speaking to TOI, Prof Rajan Kumar, professor at the School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the Ukraine conflict and the disruption of Russian gas supplies had compounded Europe's economic difficulties, particularly for Germany, which was previously a major buyer of Russian energy."Europe's economic difficulties have been compounded by the Ukraine crisis and the disruption of Russian gas supplies. Germany had planned major energy infrastructure projects, including Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2, but the pipelines were destroyed,” Rajan said.“Gas supplies were disrupted, and energy became increasingly expensive. Higher crude oil prices have added to the pressure, making energy costs unsustainable for several European economies,” he added.The economic strain has raised questions about how long European governments can sustain military assistance to Kyiv while meeting domestic spending and defence requirements. The pressure is particularly acute for countries that must simultaneously replenish their own weapons stockpiles and maintain support for Ukraine.For Russia, the challenge facing Ukraine and its European partners presents an opportunity. If Kyiv cannot secure enough interceptors before winter, Russian attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure could place further pressure on Ukraine's ability to sustain essential services. At the same time, divisions over military stockpiles and the cost of continued assistance could complicate Europe's response.

articles.title: What do Kylian Mbappe and Hello Kitty have in common? They’ve both angered China
articles.summary: What do French soccer star Kylian Mbappé and the Japanese company behind Hello Kitty have in common?
articles.body: What do French soccer star Kylian Mbappé and the Japanese company behind Hello Kitty have in common? Before this week, very little. Now, they share the unenviable position of having angered Chinese fans and consumers – then having to quickly apologize and do damage control, with big earnings on the line. It’s not the first time this has happened. In recent years, other foreign brands and prominent figures, from athletes to fashion houses, have found themselves in hot water. But this week’s back-to-back backtracks illustrate how difficult it can be to do business in China – where once you cross a perceived red line, people aren’t so quick to forgive and forget. It started when Real Madrid forward Mbappé appeared in a video posted by a French talk show, discussing a funny meme where his face had been photoshopped onto “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator.” That “guy” was former Chinese leader Mao Zedong – who, despite a tumultuous reign that saw tens of millions of deaths caused by disastrous policies, is still revered as the father of the People’s Republic. Half a century after his death, this complicated legacy is still a highly sensitive topic within China. Mbappé’s throwaway comment immediately lit a firestorm on Chinese social media, one which swiftly traveled offline. Multiple brands cut ties with him, saying they had “zero tolerance for any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.” State media removed all content and ads involving Mbappé – who came second this week in the Ballon d’Or vote for the world’s top men’s player – and halted broadcasts of all matches and events involving him and Spanish football league La Liga. Facing the threat of further repercussions, Mbappé issued a formal apology on Tuesday. “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,” he said in a statement. La Liga and other brands affiliated with Mbappé also sought to reverse the damage, emphasizing how much they valued and respected their Chinese partners. Before the furor had even died down, another was beginning – this time over Hello Kitty maker Sanrio. The company had collaborated with Japanese spy drama VIVANT to create merchandise based on Sanrio characters – including Hello Kitty, My Melody, Kuromi and Cinnamoroll – wearing outfits from the TV show. But the show had been called anti-Chinese by China’s state media amid ongoing geopolitical tensions, and the collaboration went viral on Chinese social media, where users lambasted the series for depicting Chinese intelligence agents torturing Japanese spies. By Thursday, Sanrio had backtracked, saying it had “received feedback from various parties.” “Regarding this collaboration, we believe that it contains expressions that are inconsistent with Sanrio’s corporate values. We have therefore decided to discontinue this collaboration, along with all subsequent projects and promotional activities,” it said in a statement posted both on its website and on Chinese social media platform Weibo, where a hashtag about the apology racked up more than 180 million views. Even Chinese officials weighed in. VIVANT “once again exposes the fact that there has always been a force within Japan that seeks to vilify and smear China through cultural products and spread anti-China sentiment,” said Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun in a regular press briefing on Thursday. In both cases, Sanrio and Mbappé followed a now-familiar pattern for anyone who has caused offense on Chinese social media: apologize deferentially; retract statements; discontinue controversial products; and hope it will blow over. The same sequence unfurled with Dolce & Gabbana in 2018; Versace in 2019; the Houston Rockets, and by extension the NBA, in 2019; H&M and Nike in 2021; Bulgari in 2023; and Lululemon just earlier this year. The controversies range across various topics, but many concern geopolitical or historical sensitivities, such as the status of Hong Kong and Macao as semi-autonomous regions of China, or the status of Taiwan, the self-governing democracy that Beijing views as part of its territory. Other controversies, such as the Lululemon and Sanrio ones, were fueled by historical animosity between China and Japan, with anti-Japanese sentiment gaining traction in China in recent years as bilateral ties worsen. Foreign brands or celebrities doing business in China have to tread carefully because “the Chinese consumer is hyper-sensitive to any slights or perceived slights or attacks on the Chinese country and on the Chinese people,” said Shaun Rein, founder and managing director of the China Market Research Group. “Brands have to be cautious, and they’re getting more and more so because they hire consultants and internal executives who understand historical problems and geopolitical sensitivities,” he added. This heightened online sensitivity has coincided with surging ultranationalism in recent years, as well as China’s increased assertiveness in foreign policy and territorial conflicts. Ironically, on China’s highly censored social media platforms, many outlets have not explicitly spelled out Mbappé’s comments – leading many Chinese people to wonder what he had said in the first place to hurt their feelings. But for many brands, it’s worth the risk to access China’s enormous consumer market. Sanrio China reported revenue of $117 million in the first half of 2026 alone, according to Chinese state media. The same goes for sports stars who rely on lucrative endorsements – especially in a nation already mad about basketball, and hungry for soccer. Though Western sports leagues and teams can’t publicly warn their players to avoid angering China – and risk sparking a different sort of backlash – that may well happen behind the scenes, according to sports analyst Mark Dreyer, who wrote a 2022 book about China’s sporting ambitions. “That’s just sensible business practice, particularly if you have multi-million dollar sponsorships on the line,” he told Reuters. Some controversies die down relatively quickly, and brands recover. Other times, the damage can be long-lasting – and expensive. Years after a series of racially controversial ads and offensive private messages allegedly sent by a co-founder, Dolce & Gabbana is still a label non grata in China. And after the Houston Rockets general manager voiced support for the Hong Kong pro-democracy protest movement in 2019, China severed ties with the NBA and banned all teams from playing in the country, despite copious apologies, until they were finally allowed to return last year. It’s not clear how long the road to recovery will be for Sanrio and Mbappé. But “these are the stakes of playing in China,” said Zak Dychtwald, founder of Bridgeworks Global, which advises multinational organizations. “When it goes well, everybody celebrates. And it’s the second largest economy on earth and most often your biggest growth segment for whichever company and industry you’re in,” he told Reuters. “But when you get it wrong, it could be extraordinarily painful and swift in its retribution.”
